title: The Heart and Circulation
description: The circulatory system, heart structure and how heart activity is monitored, coronary heart disease and its risk factors, blood vessels, and the components of blood for IGCSE Biology 0610 Core.

notes.heading: The Circulatory System: the Big Picture (9.1.1, 9.2.2)
notes.body:
📌 Definition (9.1.1)
A **circulatory system** is a system of **blood vessels** with a **pump** (the heart) and **valves** to ensure **one-way flow** of blood. Those four elements — vessels, pump, valves, one-way — are the definition the mark scheme expects.

🔑 Direction of flow (9.2.2)
• Blood is pumped AWAY from the heart in **arteries**.
• Blood returns TO the heart in **veins**.
• Exchange with the tissues happens in **capillaries**.

🔑 What the examiner wants
'Blood flows around the body' scores nothing. Name the vessels, the pump and the valves, and state that the valves keep the flow one-way. In diagram questions, decide 'artery' or 'vein' by DIRECTION of flow — artery means leaving the heart, even for the pulmonary artery, which carries deoxygenated blood.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Defining arteries as 'vessels that carry oxygenated blood'. The pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood, so that definition fails. Define by direction: arteries carry blood away from the heart.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Vessels + pump + valves = one-way flow.
• Arteries away, veins back, capillaries exchange.
• Single and double circulation, and why the two sides of the heart differ, are Supplement objectives — they are covered in the extended circulation topic.

notes.heading: Heart Structure: What You Must Identify (9.2.1)
notes.body:
📌 The structures to name on a front-section diagram
• **Muscular wall** — the heart is made of muscle that contracts to pump blood.
• **Septum** — the central wall separating the left and right sides.
• **Left and right atria** (singular: atrium) — the upper chambers, which RECEIVE blood.
• **Left and right ventricles** — the lower chambers, which PUMP blood out.
• **One-way valves** — between the atria and ventricles, and at the exits of the ventricles; they prevent backflow.
• **Coronary arteries** — the heart's own blood supply, branching over its surface to deliver oxygen to the heart muscle.

🔑 Diagram technique
On diagrams and photographs the heart is drawn as if the person is facing you: the heart's RIGHT side appears on the LEFT of the page. Oxygenated blood is on the heart's LEFT side. Learn the vessels with the heart: vena cava into the right atrium, pulmonary artery out of the right ventricle, pulmonary vein into the left atrium, aorta out of the left ventricle.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Labelling 'left ventricle' on the left of the diagram. Before writing left or right, find the side carrying oxygenated blood (the side joined to the aorta and pulmonary vein) — that is the heart's left.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Four chambers: atria receive, ventricles pump.
• Septum separates the sides; valves stop backflow.
• Coronary arteries feed the heart muscle itself.

illustration.alt: Front section of the heart showing the muscular wall, septum, left and right atria and ventricles, one-way valves, coronary arteries, and the vena cava, aorta, pulmonary artery and pulmonary vein.
illustration.caption: Viewed from the front, the heart's right side is on the left of the diagram: blue carries deoxygenated blood, red carries oxygenated blood.

notes.heading: Monitoring the Heart (9.2.3) and the Exercise Investigation (9.2.4)
notes.body:
📌 Three ways heart activity is monitored
• **ECG (electrocardiogram)** — a trace of the heart's electrical activity; abnormal rhythms show as abnormal traces.
• **Pulse rate** — feeling the surge of blood in an artery (wrist or neck); one pulse corresponds to one heartbeat.
• **Valve sounds** — the 'lub-dub' heard through a stethoscope is the one-way valves closing; an extra whoosh (a murmur) can indicate a leaky valve.

🔑 Required investigation: the effect of physical activity on heart rate
1. Measure the resting pulse — count the beats for a set time (and say what you did, e.g. count for 30 s and double it, or count for a full minute).
2. Do a fixed amount of exercise, such as step-ups for two minutes.
3. Measure the pulse immediately afterwards, then every minute until it returns to the resting value.
4. Repeat and average. A fitter person's pulse rises less and returns to resting sooner.
Why it rises: working muscles respire faster, so oxygen and glucose must be delivered — and carbon dioxide removed — at a higher rate.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Comparing two people's pulses without controlling the exercise. State the controls: same exercise, same duration, same counting method, and repeats. And say how you converted your count to beats per minute.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• ECG, pulse rate, valve sounds.
• Exercise → heart rate rises → returns to resting; recovery time indicates fitness.

notes.heading: Coronary Heart Disease (9.2.5–6)
notes.body:
📌 Definition (9.2.5)
**Coronary heart disease (CHD)** is caused by a **blockage of the coronary arteries**. Fatty deposits build up in the artery walls and narrow them, so the heart muscle beyond the narrowing receives less oxygen. A complete blockage starves that region of oxygen — a heart attack.

📌 The risk factors — learn the full list
• **Diet** high in saturated fat and salt
• **Lack of exercise**
• **Stress**
• **Smoking**
• **Genetic predisposition** (a family history of CHD)
• **Age** (risk rises as you get older)
• **Sex** (at a given age, risk is higher in males)

🔑 Reducing the risk (9.2.6)
The exam expects lifestyle factors linked to the mechanism: a **balanced diet** low in saturated fat and salt slows the build-up of fatty deposits, and **regular exercise** strengthens the heart muscle and keeps blood flowing well — both reduce the risk of a blockage.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Writing only 'smoking and a bad diet' when the question asks for FOUR risk factors. Age, sex and genetic predisposition cannot be changed, but they are still valid risk factors and they earn marks.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• CHD = blocked coronary arteries → less oxygen to the heart muscle.
• Seven risk factors: diet, lack of exercise, stress, smoking, genes, age, sex.
• Lower the risk: better diet, more exercise, not smoking.

notes.heading: Blood Vessels: Arteries, Veins and Capillaries (9.3)
notes.body:
📌 Structure comparison (9.3.1 — Core keeps it to three features)
• **Arteries** — **thick walls**, **narrow lumen**, no valves.
• **Veins** — **thin walls**, **wide lumen**, **valves present**.
• **Capillaries** — walls **one cell thick**, lumen barely wider than a red blood cell, no valves.

🔑 Capillary functions (9.3.2)
Capillaries form huge networks throughout every tissue and link arteries to veins. Their one-cell-thick walls give a very short diffusion distance, so oxygen and nutrients pass from the blood to the tissue cells, and carbon dioxide and other wastes pass back into the blood.

📌 The main vessels to identify (9.3.3)
• **Vena cava** — vein returning blood from the body to the right atrium.
• **Aorta** — artery carrying blood from the left ventricle to the body.
• **Pulmonary artery** — right ventricle → lungs (deoxygenated blood).
• **Pulmonary vein** — lungs → left atrium (oxygenated blood).
• **Renal artery** — carries blood from the aorta to the kidney.
• **Renal vein** — returns blood from the kidney to the vena cava.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Calling the pulmonary artery a vein because its blood is deoxygenated. Name vessels by direction: away from the heart = artery. WHY the wall thicknesses differ, and the hepatic vessels, are Supplement — see the extended circulation topic.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Thick wall + narrow lumen = artery; thin wall + wide lumen + valves = vein; one-cell wall = capillary.
• Learn the six named vessels with their direction of flow.

notes.heading: The Components of Blood (9.4.1–3)
notes.body:
📌 The four components and their functions
• **Red blood cells** — transport **oxygen**; they contain the red pigment **haemoglobin**, which binds oxygen in the lungs and releases it in respiring tissues.
• **White blood cells** — defend against pathogens: some carry out **phagocytosis** (engulfing and digesting pathogens) and others produce **antibodies**.
• **Platelets** — small cell fragments that help the blood to **clot**.
• **Plasma** — the straw-coloured liquid that transports **blood cells, ions, nutrients such as glucose and amino acids, urea, hormones and carbon dioxide**.

🔑 Identifying cells in photomicrographs (9.4.2)
Red blood cells: by far the most numerous, small, with NO visible nucleus. White blood cells: far fewer, larger, with an obvious (often lobed) nucleus. Red cells outnumber white cells by roughly a thousand to one — use numbers and size together when identifying them.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Writing that plasma 'transports oxygen'. Oxygen transport is the red blood cell's job, via haemoglobin; plasma carries dissolved substances and the cells themselves. The lymphocyte/phagocyte division of white blood cells is Supplement and is covered in the extended circulation topic.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Red = oxygen (haemoglobin); white = phagocytosis + antibodies; platelets = clotting; plasma = transport liquid.
• Micrograph ID: numerous, small, no nucleus = red; rare, large, with nucleus = white.

notes.heading: Clotting, and Exam Technique for This Topic (9.4.4)
notes.body:
📌 What clotting does
When a blood vessel is damaged, **platelets** help trigger the blood to clot. The clot has TWO protective functions, and the mark scheme wants both:
• it **prevents further blood loss** by sealing the wound, and
• it **prevents pathogens entering** the body through the break in the skin.
(The fibrinogen-to-fibrin chemistry behind the clot is Supplement and lives in the extended circulation topic.)

🔑 Exam technique for this topic
• 'Identify structure X on the heart diagram' → orient yourself first using direction of flow and which blood is oxygenated.
• 'Describe an investigation into exercise and heart rate' → give the method, the controls, the repeats, and what the recovery time shows.
• 'Compare arteries and veins' → write PAIRED statements (thick wall vs thin wall, narrow lumen vs wide lumen, valves vs no valves); an unpaired half-comparison loses the second mark.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Writing that a clot 'kills pathogens'. It does not kill them — it stops them getting in. Killing pathogens is the job of white blood cells (phagocytosis and antibodies).

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Platelets → clot → less blood loss + no pathogen entry.
• Paired comparisons, and controlled variables in the practical.

flashcards.definition: A system of blood vessels with a pump (the heart) and valves to ensure one-way flow of blood.
flashcards.example: Blood is pumped away from the heart in arteries and returns in veins.

flashcards.definition: The central muscular wall that separates the left and right sides of the heart.
flashcards.example: The septum keeps the oxygenated blood on the heart's left side apart from the deoxygenated blood on its right.

flashcards.definition: An upper chamber of the heart that receives blood — the right atrium from the vena cava, the left atrium from the pulmonary vein.
flashcards.example: The left atrium receives oxygenated blood returning from the lungs.

flashcards.definition: A lower chamber of the heart that pumps blood out — the right ventricle into the pulmonary artery, the left ventricle into the aorta.
flashcards.example: Contraction of the left ventricle sends oxygenated blood into the aorta.

flashcards.definition: The arteries branching over the heart's surface that supply the heart muscle itself with oxygenated blood.
flashcards.example: A blocked coronary artery starves part of the heart muscle of oxygen — coronary heart disease.

flashcards.definition: An electrocardiogram — a trace of the heart's electrical activity, used to monitor how the heart is working.
flashcards.example: An irregular heart rhythm shows up as an abnormal ECG trace.

flashcards.definition: Disease caused by blockage of the coronary arteries by fatty deposits, reducing oxygen supply to the heart muscle.
flashcards.example: Risk factors include a fatty diet, lack of exercise, stress, smoking, genetic predisposition, age and sex.

flashcards.definition: A vessel carrying blood away from the heart, with a thick wall and a narrow lumen.
flashcards.example: The aorta carries oxygenated blood from the left ventricle to the body.

flashcards.definition: A vessel returning blood to the heart, with a thin wall, a wide lumen and valves.
flashcards.example: The vena cava returns deoxygenated blood from the body to the right atrium.

flashcards.definition: A microscopic vessel with walls one cell thick, forming networks where substances are exchanged between blood and tissue cells.
flashcards.example: Oxygen and glucose leave the blood through capillary walls in the muscles.

flashcards.definition: The red pigment inside red blood cells that binds oxygen in the lungs and releases it in the tissues.
flashcards.example: Oxygen transport in the blood is carried out by haemoglobin, not by the plasma.

flashcards.definition: The liquid part of blood, transporting blood cells, ions, nutrients, urea, hormones and carbon dioxide.
flashcards.example: Urea travels in the plasma from the liver to the kidneys for excretion.

questions.stem: A circulatory system is best described as:
choices: A network of neurones carrying impulses to the heart
A system of blood vessels with a pump and valves to ensure one-way flow of blood
The heart alone, pumping blood in all directions
A system of air tubes and a pump moving gases around the body
questions.explanation: The syllabus definition has four parts: blood vessels, a pump, valves, and one-way flow. Neurones belong to the nervous system, and the heart without vessels and valves is not a circulatory system.

questions.stem: By definition, an artery is a blood vessel that:
choices: Carries oxygenated blood
Carries blood towards the heart
Has the thinnest wall of any vessel
Carries blood away from the heart
questions.explanation: Arteries are defined by direction — they carry blood away from the heart. 'Oxygenated blood' fails because the pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood to the lungs; veins carry blood towards the heart.

questions.stem: Which chamber of the heart pumps blood into the aorta?
choices: Left ventricle
Right ventricle
Left atrium
Right atrium
questions.explanation: Ventricles pump blood out of the heart, and the left ventricle pumps oxygenated blood into the aorta for the body. The right ventricle pumps into the pulmonary artery; atria receive blood rather than pumping it out.

questions.stem: What is the main function of red blood cells?
choices: Helping the blood to clot
Producing antibodies
Transporting oxygen, bound to haemoglobin
Engulfing pathogens by phagocytosis
questions.explanation: Red blood cells transport oxygen using the pigment haemoglobin. Clotting is the role of platelets, while antibody production and phagocytosis are white blood cell functions.

questions.stem: In a photomicrograph of blood, a student sees thousands of small cells with no nucleus and a few much larger cells with lobed nuclei. What are the larger cells?
choices: Red blood cells
Platelets
White blood cells
Plasma proteins
questions.explanation: White blood cells are larger, far less numerous and have an obvious nucleus; red blood cells are small, nucleus-free and vastly more numerous. Platelets are tiny cell fragments, and plasma proteins are not cells at all.

questions.stem: Which statement about the pulmonary artery is correct?
choices: It carries deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle to the lungs
It carries oxygenated blood from the lungs to the heart
It is really a vein, because it carries deoxygenated blood
It carries blood from the heart to the kidneys
questions.explanation: The pulmonary artery leaves the right ventricle for the lungs carrying deoxygenated blood — it is an artery because it carries blood AWAY from the heart. Vessels are named by direction, not by how oxygenated the blood is.

questions.stem: A valve between the left atrium and the left ventricle fails to close properly. What is the direct result when the ventricle contracts?
choices: Blood stops flowing through the heart altogether
The muscular wall of the ventricle tears
Blood flows into the aorta faster than usual
Some blood flows backwards into the left atrium
questions.explanation: One-way valves prevent backflow. If the valve between atrium and ventricle cannot close, ventricular contraction pushes some blood back up into the atrium instead of sending it all into the aorta — this is what a heart murmur can indicate.

questions.stem: Which change would reduce a person's risk of coronary heart disease?
choices: Increasing the amount of salt and saturated fat in the diet
Taking regular exercise and eating a balanced diet low in saturated fat
Cutting out all fats and carbohydrates from the diet
Relying on being young, since CHD only affects older people
questions.explanation: A balanced diet slows the build-up of fatty deposits in the coronary arteries, and regular exercise strengthens the heart — both reduce CHD risk. Age is a risk factor but not protection, and extreme diets are not the recommended change.

questions.stem: Two students do the same two-minute step test. Student A's pulse returns to its resting value within 2 minutes; student B's takes 6 minutes. What is the best conclusion?
choices: B is fitter, because their heart worked harder
A's heart is weaker, so it recovers sooner
The test is invalid — pulse rate cannot indicate fitness
A is likely to be fitter — a fitter person's heart rate rises less and returns to resting sooner
questions.explanation: With the exercise controlled, recovery time is the comparison: a fitter heart meets the muscles' demand more easily, so the pulse rises less and settles back faster. A slow return to resting suggests lower fitness, not harder work.

questions.stem: Capillary networks in muscle tissue allow rapid exchange between blood and tissue cells. Which features make this possible?
choices: Thick muscular walls and a wide lumen
Valves that push substances out of the blood
Walls only one cell thick, giving a very short diffusion distance, and a huge total surface area
High pressure that forces red blood cells out into the tissues
questions.explanation: Capillaries trade strength for exchange: walls one cell thick minimise the diffusion path, and the branching network gives an enormous surface area. Thick walls belong to arteries, capillaries have no valves, and red blood cells never leave the blood.

questions.stem: Which of these vessels carries deoxygenated blood?
choices: Aorta
Pulmonary artery
Pulmonary vein
Renal artery
questions.explanation: The pulmonary artery is the exception that tests the rule: it is an artery (blood away from the heart) but carries deoxygenated blood to the lungs. The aorta, pulmonary vein and renal artery all carry oxygenated blood.

questions.stem: Which substance is transported dissolved in the blood plasma?
choices: Urea
Oxygen
Haemoglobin
Platelets
questions.explanation: Plasma transports dissolved substances including ions, nutrients, urea, hormones and carbon dioxide, plus the blood cells themselves. Oxygen travels bound to haemoglobin inside red blood cells, and platelets are cell fragments, not a dissolved substance.

questions.stem: What is the role of platelets?
choices: Transporting carbon dioxide to the lungs
Helping the blood to clot at a wound
Carrying oxygen to respiring tissues
Making antibodies against pathogens
questions.explanation: Platelets are cell fragments that help trigger clotting when a vessel is damaged — the clot prevents further blood loss and blocks pathogens from entering. Oxygen transport is done by red blood cells; antibodies come from white blood cells.

questions.stem: The 'lub-dub' sounds a doctor hears through a stethoscope are produced by:
choices: The heart's one-way valves closing
Blood squirting through the aorta
The lungs inflating with each heartbeat
The coronary arteries pulsing
questions.explanation: Valve sounds are one of the three ways heart activity is monitored (with ECG and pulse rate): each heartbeat makes the one-way valves snap shut, producing the characteristic sounds. An extra whoosh suggests a leaky valve.

questions.stem: A small cut in the skin clots within minutes. Beyond preventing blood loss, why does the clot matter?
choices: It kills the pathogens already inside the wound
It releases antibodies into the surrounding skin
It seals the wound so pathogens cannot enter the body
It carries extra oxygen to the damaged tissue
questions.explanation: Clotting has two protective functions: preventing blood loss AND preventing pathogens entering through the broken skin. A clot does not kill pathogens — that is the job of white blood cells, by phagocytosis and antibody production.
